archetype.name: Rebuilding
archetype.definition: A team in its second straight season at the bottom of the site's rankings, out-chanced nightly and without the goaltending or blueline to hide it, playing young skaters through the losses.

report.headline: Worst underlying play in the league, and the goaltending makes it worse
report.take:
Vancouver is 3-15-1, last in the Pacific and 32nd of 32 on the site, and this is not a slump. Last season ended 25-49-8 with 58 points and the same 32nd-place site rank, and the 5-on-5 numbers have slipped since then. Their xGF % of .399 ranks last in the league, down from .442 a year ago. They take 21.8 shots a game, fewest in the league, and allow 31, second-most. The goal differential of -32 over 19 games comes straight out of those shot counts.

Three things stack on top of the shot problem. The goaltending is last in the league by save % (.859) and by Goalies GSAx (-14.6), and nearly all of that damage traces to Kevin Lankinen, who has an .808 save % and -15 GSAx in his eight starts. Leevi Merilainen's .889 is close to the league's .891. The penalty kill stops 63.5%, 31st and far below the league's 77%. The defense also concedes points to opposing forwards at a rate no other team allows (rank 32 against forwards, wingers and defensemen alike). The blueline grades F. Filip Hronek logs 26 minutes a night at -14, and Zeev Buium plays 21 minutes while ranking 241st of 252 defensemen.

The record and the goal differential don't fully agree. Their Pts vs Goal Diff of -5.9 is the league's worst, so close games and overtime have gone against them even beyond what the margins imply. The one figure flattering them is finishing: a 13.3% shooting rate, 4th in the league against an 11.6% average, is the only reason a team that shoots this little ranks 24th in scoring rather than last. Some of the bad luck should come back, and so should some of the good. The net effect is a team that should collect points a little faster than its current pace of 30 but still sits at or near the bottom.

The recent form shows no turn yet. They are 0-5 over the last five and 1-9 over the last ten, and the only win in that stretch was a 6-5 overtime game at Anaheim. Elias Pettersson (19 points, 46th of 233 centers) and Brock Boeser (7 goals, 9 PP points) carry what offense there is. Jonathan Lekkerimaki (14 points) and Liam Ohgren (6 goals) are the most encouraging part of the season, and for a rebuilding team that is what this season is for.

strengths.title: Finishing what little they generate
strengths.body: Vancouver converts 13.3% of its shots, 4th in the league and well above the league's 11.6%. That is why a team with the fewest shots a game still sits mid-pack-low in scoring rather than last. Rates that far above average on this little volume rarely hold, so expect the goal output to slide unless the shot totals rise.

strengths.title: Pettersson and Boeser drive the scoring
strengths.body: Pettersson's 19 points rank him 46th of 233 centers despite a .428 xGF %. Boeser has 7 goals and 9 power-play points and is the main reason the PP (20.7%) sits close to the league's 22.5% instead of with the rest of the team's bottom-tier numbers. The top-end production is real, but it rests on two players, and both are losing their minutes at even strength.

strengths.title: Young wingers are producing
strengths.body: Lekkerimaki has 14 points in about 15 minutes a night and ranks 60th of 129 right wingers. Ohgren has 6 goals. For a rebuilding team that is a meaningful return, though both sit below .420 xGF %, so the production is coming despite the territory, not because of it.

concerns.title: Out-shot and out-chanced every night
concerns.body: An xGF % of .399 and a CF % of .44 put them last and 30th at 5-on-5. They allow 31 shots a game while managing 21.8, and the defense is ranked last against forwards, wingers and defensemen alike. This is structural and consistent with last season's .442, so it is the part least likely to correct itself.

concerns.title: Lankinen's starts are sinking them
concerns.body: The team's .859 save % and -14.6 GSAx are both last in the league. Lankinen accounts for essentially all of it: .808 and -15 GSAx, 69th of 69 goalies. Merilainen at .889 is roughly league average, so the more starts he gets, the more the goals-against number should come down toward merely bad.

concerns.title: A penalty kill that barely functions
concerns.body: The kill succeeds 63.5% of the time, 31st and far below the league's 77%. Weak goaltending feeds part of it, and some recovery is likely. Still, with this blueline (graded F, Hronek -14 in 26 minutes a night), even a correction leaves it a liability.

trend.note: A 2-13 October gave way to an 0-3 start to November. They have lost five straight and are 1-9 in their last ten, with the last five running well below even their poor season points rate.

weekAhead.headline: One winnable home game, then three against better teams
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with the best chance they will get: Philadelphia at home, a 4-10-5 team ranked 30th whose offense is 31st and shoots just 9.2%. After that it gets steep. The Rangers arrive with A+ goaltending, a .911 save % and the league's 2nd-best penalty kill. Then Vancouver plays a road back-to-back at Vegas (5th on the site, 2nd at holding forwards under their averages) and Utah.

Utah is the odd matchup. Its xGF % is 2nd in the league and its power play converts 37.1%, which is a nightmare for a 63.5% kill. But its goaltending grades F with an .871 save %, so a Vancouver team that finishes well could trade chances there. Realistically this is a one-win week, with Philadelphia the game that has to be it.

keyMatchups.title: Philadelphia: the must-have game
keyMatchups.body: The Flyers can't score: their offense ranks 31st and they shoot 9.2%. Their defense does give up the 30th-most points to defensemen, which is an opening for Hronek's power-play touches. If Vancouver can't beat a 30th-ranked team at home, the losing streak runs through the week.

keyMatchups.title: Utah's power play against Vancouver's kill
keyMatchups.body: Utah converts 37.1% of its power plays, 2nd in the league, against a kill working at 63.5%. Staying out of the box matters more in this game than any other this week. Utah's .871 save % is the one opening for Vancouver's 4th-ranked finishing.

keyMatchups.title: Low volume against elite goaltending
keyMatchups.body: The Rangers allow just 23.2 shots a game and save .911. Vegas holds forwards under their averages better than all but one team. For a team that already takes the fewest shots in the league, these two games test whether the hot shooting survives against real goaltending.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal, especially across the Vegas-Utah back-to-back: Merilainen has been close to league average, Lankinen has not.

restOfSeason.body:
Vancouver is a bottom-two team the rest of the way, but the 30-point pace understates it. The Pts vs Goal Diff of -5.9 is the worst in the league and should drift back toward zero. A goaltending split leaning on Merilainen rather than Lankinen would also pull goals against down from 4.58 a game, and the penalty kill can hardly stay this far below average. Working against that, 13.3% shooting on the league's lowest shot volume won't hold, so the offense likely gets worse before it gets better.

Net, expect a points rate closer to last season's than to this one's but no better, something like 17 to 24 wins and 42 to 56 points. Nothing in the shot or chance numbers suggests a climb out of the Pacific's basement. The season's real measure is the development of Lekkerimaki, Ohgren, Buium and Willander, and whether the 5-on-5 share moves off .399.

confidence.note: 19 games is a small sample, but the poor shot and chance shares match last season.
